ECE 6390

Differential and π/4 phase encoding

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the class DQPSK example, where words 11, 10, 00 and 01 move the phase from 0° to 90°, 90°, 0° and 180°, and the same sequence after an unknown 37° rotation, which leaves every phase change intact.

Coherent QPSK maps each two-bit word to an absolute phase, so the receiver must know the carrier phase. Differential QPSK (DQPSK) maps each word to a phase change instead: φₖ = φₖ₋₁ + Δφₖ, with a reference symbol supplying the first phase. The class convention is 10 → 0°, 11 → +90°, 00 → −90° and 01 → 180°.

The receiver multiplies each received value by the conjugate of the previous one: rₖr*ₖ₋₁ = Eₛe^(j(Δφₖ − εₖ + εₖ₋₁)). A constant unknown carrier phase ε cancels, so no absolute phase estimate is needed. A frequency offset still adds a phase step of 2πΔfTₛ per symbol, and symbol timing is still required.

The convenience costs detection performance. The previous symbol is noisy too, so differential detection compares two noisy samples and needs more Eb/N₀ than coherent detection at the same error rate; for DQPSK the penalty is roughly 2 to 3 dB at low error rates.

π/4-DQPSK uses the changes ±45° and ±135°. Successive symbols alternate between the 0°/90° set and a set rotated by 45°, giving eight possible locations but still four choices per symbol, so two bits per symbol. No step passes through 180°, which keeps the signal trajectory away from the origin. A fixed 45° rotation of ordinary QPSK, by contrast, changes nothing about its spacing or performance.

Example

Starting from 0°, words 11, 10, 00 and 01 give phases 90°, 90°, 0° and 180°. If the channel rotates every received point by 37°, the received phases are 53°, 53°, −37° and 143° after a reference at −37°, and their successive differences are still +90°, 0°, −90° and +180°, so every word decodes correctly.

Practice

1. Using the class DQPSK mapping and a 0° reference, which phases follow the words 01, 01, 11?

Add each word’s phase change to the previous phase.

01 adds 180°, giving 180°; the next 01 adds 180°, giving 360° = 0°; 11 adds 90°, giving 90°.

2. Why can a 50° per-symbol phase drift break DQPSK decisions even though a constant rotation cannot?

Compare the drift with the 45° half-spacing between allowed phase changes.

A constant rotation cancels between consecutive symbols, but a drift adds 50° to every measured change. That pushes each measurement past the 45° midpoint toward the neighbouring allowed change, so the decoder picks the wrong word.
